title: Embryos of different animals in the same class are strikingly similar

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Embryos of different animals in the same class are strikingly similar

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Embryos of distinct animals within the same class are often strikingly similar, more so than the adults, and the points of resemblance often have no direct relation to their conditions of existence.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The embryos, also, of distinct animals within the same class are often strikingly similar

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIII, “Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs”; section “EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age”. Scope: animals within the same class, especially vertebrates and insects

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch13-16: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.61

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Morphological similarity through ontogeny has a clear quantitative test. Existing public data cover selected vertebrates and insects, not the stated breadth.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use stage-matched embryo images or landmark data to compare within-class interspecific morphological distances during development with adult distances and test association with ecological conditions. Lower embryonic than adult disparity and weak embryo-environment association support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Developmental stages are difficult to align across species.

Open embryo imaging is concentrated in model organisms rather than whole classes.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Embryo-versus-adult distance is a clear criterion, and public expression archives plus specimen imagery can support it for small sets of vertebrates. That is a restricted scope relative to animals within a class. The comparison can discriminate the claim from ecology-driven embryonic resemblance, but assembling comparable stages across more than a handful of species is slow specialist work.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Within classes, compare multivariate morphological or transcriptomic distances among species at matched embryonic stages and at adult stages, and test whether embryonic similarity is independent of habitat similarity. The claim is confirmed if embryos of a class cluster more tightly than adults and embryonic closeness does not track shared conditions, and refuted if adults are as similar as embryos or embryonic resemblance follows ecology.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Matched embryonic stages exist mainly for model vertebrates and a few insects, not for animals of a whole class.

Staging landmarks are not equivalent across phyla, so an 'early' stage in one group is not the same comparison in another.

Transcriptome studies often find a mid-development hourglass rather than uniform embryonic similarity, which the morphometric data must be allowed to show.
